interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through what happens, layer by layer, when you type a URL and hit enter.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd structure this top-down through TCP/IP's four layers rather than trying to name all seven OSI layers: application builds an HTTP request; transport (TCP) breaks it into segments and adds source/destination ports; internet (IP) adds source/destination addresses and figures out routing; link wraps it in a frame addressed to the next hop's MAC and puts it on the wire.

Concretely: your browser (application) forms `GET / HTTP/1.1`; TCP wraps it in a segment tagged with port 443; IP wraps that in a packet tagged with the server's address; Ethernet wraps that in a frame addressed to your default gateway's MAC, since the destination is off-LAN. Each layer only adds a header — it never touches what's already inside.

**Testing:** whether you understand encapsulation as the mechanism connecting the layers, not just memorized layer names.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Layer-by-layer request walkthrough

interviewQuestions.question: Why do we still teach OSI if the internet doesn't actually run on it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd say OSI survives as a **shared vocabulary**, not an implementation. Saying "that's a layer 2 problem" instantly tells another engineer to look at switches and MAC addresses rather than routing tables — it's a fast way to scope a conversation or a bug.

For example, when debugging "the site is down," asking "is this layer 3 (routing) or layer 7 (the app returning errors)" narrows the investigation immediately, even though no software module is literally called "layer 3." TCP/IP is what's deployed; OSI is the shared map everyone uses to talk about it precisely.

**Testing:** whether you see OSI as a communication and diagnostic tool rather than a rival implementation to TCP/IP.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why OSI still matters
